extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, regulators, legal practitioners, employers, worker advocates, and researchers engaged with FTC rulemaking on non-competes
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of evidence and public comments assessing how worker non-compete agreements affect competition, wages, job quality, new business formation, and innovation for purposes of an FTC rulemaking determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppressed earnings due to non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes inhibit efficient matching between workers and employers and thereby suppress workers' earnings (both initial earnings and earnings growth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites empirical literature (natural experiments and other studies) finding lower earnings where non-competes are more enforceable (e.g., Treasury report, Johnson/Lavetti/Lipsitz). Commenter anecdotes corroborate harms. The Commission gives weight to studies showing negative effects across income levels and uses conservative assumptions in its regulatory impact analysis (it assumes prohibition has effects similar to observed incremental legal changes rather than extrapolating to larger effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence weighting: study design matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate empirical studies based on methodology: greater weight is given to natural experiments and stronger causal designs than to cross-sectional/enforceability-correlational studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission prefers studies that can support causal inference (natural experiments, before/after with individual-level comparisons like Lipsitz & Starr). Cross-sectional studies of enforceability receive less weight because they cannot distinguish causality. Where studies differ, assess internal validity concerns (confounders, measurement error, external validity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity and conservative extrapolation in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing magnitude, consider whether effects of changes in enforceability are broadly linear; linearity can justify extrapolation from incremental legal changes to larger reforms, but regulatory analyses can choose conservative assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson, Lavetti, and Lipsitz find broadly linear effects; the Commission views extrapolation as appropriate in interpretation but follows a conservative approach in the regulatory impact analysis by not extrapolating beyond incremental observed changes, thereby likely underestimating benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competes degrade working conditions (job quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes prevent workers from escaping poor working conditions or demanding improvements, leading to degraded job quality (unsafe, abusive, toxic workplaces, discrimination, wage theft, denied benefits, burnout, mental and physical health harms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large volume of qualitative comments describing specific harms (examples: threats in journalism, pregnancy discrimination, abusive employers, excessive on-call hours, stress-related health problems, suicide risk in healthcare). Commission treats this qualitative evidence as bolstering findings on competitive harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competes inhibit labor mobility and efficient matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes restrain workers' ability to switch jobs or start businesses, reducing efficient matching between workers' skills and employer opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced matching is a channel for suppressed earnings and reduced innovation. Empirical studies that measure changes in mobility after legal changes are especially informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inhibited new business formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes reduce the rate of new firm entry and deter spinoffs and entrepreneurship, thereby harming competition in product and service markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several empirical studies (e.g., Jeffers, Marx, Johnson/Lipsitz/Pei) document declines in new firm entry when enforceability increases; effects can be larger for women. Study design quality affects weight; Commission cites studies that satisfy methodology principles highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced innovation due to worker restraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes tend to reduce innovation by (1) preventing workers from starting businesses to pursue new ideas, (2) inhibiting efficient matching so talent isn't used optimally, and (3) reducing worker movement and knowledge flow between firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovation metrics include new products/services, improvements, and cross-firm knowledge diffusion. Commission relies on empirical and qualitative evidence showing these three mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased market concentration, higher consumer prices, and reduced product quality
rubrics_metrics.description: By limiting new entrants and firm growth, non-competes tend to increase market concentration, which can raise consumer prices and lower product quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites empirical and qualitative evidence linking non-competes to higher concentration and consumer harms; these market-level harms bolster findings under Section 5 even where direct worker harms are primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity in magnitude but directional consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Although estimated magnitudes of non-compete effects vary across worker groups, occupations, industries, and geographies, the effects are directionally similar (generally negative) across diverse subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission notes studies showing larger adverse effects for college-educated and occupations with high non-compete use, but still negative effects for other workers (e.g., Lipsitz & Starr for lower-wage workers). Assess subgroup analyses but recognize consistent negative direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competes exacerbate racial and gender wage gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence indicates non-competes decrease entrepreneurship and wages disproportionately for women and people of color, thereby widening wage gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission references studies and many commenter accounts; it does not solely rest its unfair-competition finding on this but considers these distributional harms as corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competes chill reporting, whistleblowing, and collective action
rubrics_metrics.description: By restricting post-employment opportunities, non-competes reduce the likelihood that workers report fraud, harassment, wage theft, or participate in union activities, and increase potential for retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters and organizations provided survey/case evidence; legal protections for whistleblowers may come too late if workers cannot find other employment. Consider impacts on NLRA-protected activity and enforcement incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of enforceability indices and enforcement-outcome evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: State-level enforceability indices—based on qualitative legal analyses across multiple dimensions—are sufficiently reliable to inform inference, and enforcement-outcome studies provide additional corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While indices may have measurement error concerns, careful construction mitigates this. Newer studies using enforcement outcomes (e.g., 2024 Washington study) align with index-based findings; use both types of evidence together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 legal standard: tendency to negatively affect competition suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 5 of the FTC Act, demonstrating that conduct tends to negatively affect competitive conditions is sufficient to establish an unfair method of competition; empirical proof of actual harm is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission applies this legal standard, relying on the tendency shown by empirical studies and qualitative comments; thus a preponderance of directional evidence and mechanisms can support a rule even absent proof of realized aggregate harm in every instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competes harm workers across wage levels (not only low-wage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical and comment evidence show non-competes suppress earnings and/or harm conditions for both lower-wage and many higher-wage (non-senior-executive) workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission rejects claims that only low-wage workers are harmed; evidence shows negative effects for a range of earnings levels. Consider occupational context and bargaining power but do not assume protections only benefit low-wage workers.
